v2_codex_lo = min(s.median_seconds for s in codex_runners)
v2_codex_hi = max(s.median_seconds for s in codex_runners)

v3_codex_hi = max(s.median_seconds for s in v3.values() if s.model.startswith("gpt"))

review_lo = f"{min(review_scores):.1f}"
review_hi = f"{max(review_scores):.1f}"

deltas = r.v2_v3_deltas
def _signed(d: int) -> str:
    return f"+{d}" if d > 0 else ("0" if d == 0 else f"-{abs(d)}")
delta_line = ", ".join(
    f"{name} {_signed(d)}"
    for name, d in sorted(deltas.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])
)
moved_count = sum(1 for d in deltas.values() if d != 0)
delta_sum = _signed(sum(deltas.values()))

luna_path = ", ".join(str(r.gate_by_board["luna"][b]) for b in BOARD_ORDER)
terra_path = ", ".join(str(r.gate_by_board["terra"][b]) for b in BOARD_ORDER)

v2f = r.v2_fable
v3f_timeout = r.v3_fable_timeout
case04_passers = " and ".join(r.case04_v3_passers)

fable_out_tokens = f"{fable3.output_tokens:,}"


def table(
    headers: list[str],
    rows: list[list[str]],
    caption: str = "",
    colwidths: list[int] | None = None,
) -> Markdown:
    lines = [
        "| " + " | ".join(headers) + " |",
        "|" + "|".join("---" for _ in headers) + "|",
    ]
    lines += ["| " + " | ".join(row) + " |" for row in rows]
    if caption:
        attrs = (
            " {tbl-colwidths=\"[" + ",".join(map(str, colwidths)) + "]\"}"
            if colwidths
            else ""
        )
        lines += ["", f": {caption}{attrs}"]
    return Markdown("\n".join(lines))

## Introduction

The Axiom Foundation publishes statutes as executable code. An AI encoder
drafts each encoding in RuleSpec — parameters and formulas that cite their
statutory authority, carry their effective dates, and ship with companion
tests — and a deterministic gauntlet decides what merges. That design turns
model choice into an engineering question with money and correctness
attached: which model drafts law-as-code well enough to sit inside a
production pipeline, and how would you know?

EncodeBench makes the question measurable. It formalizes the informal
bake-off the Axiom Foundation ran in July 2026 to route its own encoder,
replacing a scratchpad comparison with a pinned suite, a deterministic
fold, and public records. Code benchmarks grade models on tests
[@chen2021humaneval; @jimenez2024swebench] and legal benchmarks grade them
on reasoning tasks [@guha2023legalbench]; encoding law sits at the seam,
where the output is code and the ground truth is a statute. Languages built
for that ground truth [@merigoux2021catala] and rules-as-code programs in
government [@mohun2020cracking] define the target; EncodeBench measures who
can hit it. Its sister benchmark PolicyBench [@policybench2026] asks whether
a model can compute the law; EncodeBench asks whether it can write it.

Three boards in, the results worth the most attention concern the
measurement itself. Between two full-roster runs a day apart, five of six
models moved, and the movement skewed positive — so a single board reads as
one sample, not a ranking. A read-only audit found the three encoder
backends administering different exams. The setting that appeared to pin
reasoning effort did nothing on any backend. Each finding carries a
disclosure against the boards it affects, each fix landed in the open, and
the same deterministic machinery that grades the models caught every one of
them. The paper reports the boards together with everything known to weaken
them, then pre-registers the run that removes the weaknesses.

## The task

One case gives one model one provision. The harness resolves the provision's
text from a signed corpus release — every run here pins
`{python} r.corpus_release`, verified against its publishing key — and
places it in a cold workspace: the source text, stubs for defined terms, and
no existing encoding of the target. The model writes the RuleSpec module:
the parameters and formulas the provision defines, citations back to it,
effective dates, and the companion tests the repository requires of every
rule. The suite covers UK law because the UK repository reached the signed-release
toolchain the eval requires first; a US suite follows its release migration.

Capability cases run cold for a reason. A workspace with repository context
includes whatever encoding of the provision already merged, so a capability
score would come to measure copying, and would drift as the repository
grows. Cold workspaces still carry definition stubs and canonical-concept
context, identically for every model. The last three cases run with
repository context as oracle candidates: they sit on the PolicyEngine UK
comparison path and will carry a live oracle check once that plumbing is
verified for eval cases; until then they grade on the same deterministic
gates as everything else.

Two cases exist to catch invented numbers. `child_benefit_entitlement`
supplies entitlement conditions whose weekly amounts live in a different
instrument — the 2006 regulations — so any rate literal in that encoding is
an invention. `finance_act_2026_charge` encodes an act that postdates most
of the roster's training data, so the encoding must come from the supplied
text rather than recall.

## Four gates and a fold

A case passes for a model only when four deterministic checks pass: the
encode returns an artifact, the artifact compiles in the Axiom rules engine,
repository validation passes — including the companion tests — and the
grounding scan finds zero numeric literals absent from the source text. The
gate-pass count is the headline, and nothing else folds into it.

Everything else reports alongside. A pinned reviewer model scores each
encoding's statutory fidelity — a single, noisy judge, and one whose own
family competes on the board, so it cannot referee neutrally and its score
sits beside the gates rather than inside them. On board v3 its mean
scores span `{python} review_lo` to `{python} review_hi` of 10 across all
six runners — a band too narrow to separate the leaders, which is why it
never gets to try. The oracle column stays empty until the PolicyEngine UK
runtime path is verified for eval cases. Latency and cost report as
measured.

The roster carries a control: `gpt-5.6-luna`, which prior internal
measurement found weak at exactly this task. Across the three boards it
scored `{python} luna_path` of 16 — at or near the bottom every time. A
board that failed to separate the control from the leaders would indict the
instrument, not the models.

Runs fold into one board only when the suite name, the ordered case
identities, the corpus release, and the normalized score-affecting toolchain
identity all match. Runner sets may differ — a model added later folds
cleanly without re-running incumbents — but a changed encoder refuses to
fold: a new toolchain starts a new board by construction. Two of this
paper's findings turn on that refusal.

Three readings of the current board survive the variance analysis that
follows; the rest wait for board v4.

First, the extremes separate. `gpt-5.5` and `gpt-5.6-sol` clear
`{python} g553.gate_label` and `{python} sol3.gate_label` while the control
and `claude-opus-5` sit at `{python} v3["luna"].gate_label` and
`{python} v3["opus-5"].gate_label` — gaps far wider than anything the
run-to-run movement produced.

Second, no model invented a number. Across the
`{python} r.artifacts_all_boards` artifacts produced over all three boards,
the grounding scan found `{python} r.ungrounded_artifacts_all_boards` with
an ungrounded numeric — the two trap cases included. Frontier models do not
fail this suite by fabricating rates; they fail it by writing encodings
whose tests prove them wrong. The verification burden this implies sits in
test quality, not fact-checking literals.

Third, speed and cost split by family, not by score. The codex runners'
median case ran `{python} v3_codex_lo`–`{python} v3_codex_hi` seconds on v3;
fable's ran `{python} fable3.median_seconds` seconds and emitted
`{python} fable_out_tokens` output tokens, putting its suite cost at
`{python} r.money(fable3.cost)` against `{python} r.money(sol3.cost)` for
sol — `{python} r.fable_cost_multiple_of_sol`× the cost for a lower score
on this board.

## What it takes to measure this honestly

### Scores bind to the toolchain {#sec-variance}

Between board v2 (encoder 0.2.1380, `{python} r.run_date("v2")`) and board
v3 (0.2.1382, `{python} r.run_date("v3")`), gate-pass moved
`{python} delta_line` — `{python} str(moved_count)` of six models moved,
net `{python} delta_sum`. Movement that skewed positive rules out symmetric
run-to-run noise as the whole story. Two causes confound, and two runs
cannot separate them: model nondeterminism, and real toolchain change — the
validator gained typed numeric occurrences and a locale profile between the
boards, alongside the timeout fix. The fold's refusal to combine boards
across encoder versions stopped looking like bookkeeping here and started
doing its job.

Four consequences govern how to read any single board:

- **A board is one sample.** gpt-5.5 leads v3 at
  `{python} g553.gate_label` with sol at `{python} sol3.gate_label` — one
  case apart, from a model that moved four cases between boards. The order
  of ranks one and two is not a finding.
- **The extremes are findings.** The gaps separating the leaders from the
  control and from opus-5 exceed every delta the rerun produced.
- **A score is citable only with its encoder version.** This paper writes
  encoder versions next to every number for that reason, and the fold
  refuses to blend versions mechanically.
- **The one ranking result that reproduced: terra below sol.** terra scored
  `{python} terra_path` across the boards — the steadiest line any model
  produced — while sol scored `{python} sol_path`. Two six-model boards on
  different toolchains and the four-model pilot agree. The July bake-off
  this benchmark formalizes had read the two as interchangeable on a
  smaller, easier case set; the finding that survives every board is that
  the larger, colder suite separates them.

### A timeout that graded slowness as failure {#sec-timeout}

Board v2's harness carried a hardcoded 600-second ceiling on the Claude
encoder path. The codex path exposed configurable timeouts; the Claude path
hardcoded one constant that nobody had reason to read. fable's median case
ran `{python} fable2.median_seconds` seconds on that board — roughly four
to seven times the codex runners' `{python} v2_codex_lo`–`{python} v2_codex_hi` —
so the ceiling truncated exactly one model's tail. The harness killed
`{python} str(v2f["killed"])` of its sixteen cases with no artifact
produced, and the fold scored each absent artifact as a compile and
grounding miss. Among the `{python} str(v2f["completed"])` cases that
completed, fable passed `{python} str(v2f["completed_passes"])`. The board
record flagged the row as a floor the day it posted, and this paper does
not cite it as a capability number anywhere.

The fix replaced the constant with a configurable, recorded budget —
uniform 1,800 seconds per encoder invocation and 3,600 per case on v3 — and
made timeouts visible: a case that exhausts its budget records
`timed_out`, renders as T on the grid, and drops out of the artifact
denominators instead of masquerading as a bad encoding. Execution identity
now carries the timeout policy, so runs under different ceilings refuse to
fold, the same way different encoders do.

Board v3 exercised the whole path on real artifacts. All six runners
finalized with no operator salvage — on v2, two of six needed manual
recovery after compile-failure text embedded ephemeral staging paths, a
reproducibility defect the same fix normalized — and the board's one
timeout, fable's `{python} v3f_timeout["case"]` at
`{python} f"{v3f_timeout['seconds']:,}"` seconds of case budget, reads as
exactly what it is.

### The effort setting that did nothing {#sec-effort}

Every board above ran with a harness line that appeared to pin codex
reasoning effort: `-c reasoning_effort="low"` on every codex invocation.
`reasoning_effort` is not a recognized Codex configuration field — the real
key is `model_reasoning_effort` — and codex invoked without
`--strict-config` accepts unknown keys silently. The line never did
anything. Every codex runner on every board ran at its receiver default,
and the Claude path passes no effort flag at all, so those runners did too.
A note posted to the tracking issue first reported the runs as pinned to
low effort; receiver verification the same day corrected the record to
inert. As a defect class this is worse than a wrong setting: the source
reads as though the comparison is controlled.

A five-sample-per-level probe established what each knob does. On codex,
the recognized key moves real resources: gpt-5.6-terra's median reasoning
tokens rose from `{python} f"{probe_lo['median']:.0f}"` at low to
`{python} f"{probe_xhigh['median']:.0f}"` at xhigh, median wall time from
`{python} str(probe_lo["wall_s"])`s to `{python} str(probe_xhigh["wall_s"])`s,
and ultra ran slowest (`{python} str(probe_ultra["wall_s"])`s median) with
the widest spread
(`{python} f"{min(probe_ultra['all']):.0f}–{max(probe_ultra['all']):.0f}"`
reasoning tokens). On the Claude CLI, `--effort` changed nothing measurable
in print mode: cost, wall time, and answers held flat from low through max,
and claude-opus-5 returned the same answer at every level — consistent
with the Claude 5 family regulating its own reasoning depth.

Cross-family effort matching therefore has no honest implementation on
these receivers. The design that survives is asymmetric and says so: sweep
the codex arms at declared, receiver-verified levels; run the Claude arms
at their adaptive default and label them that way. Board v4 records
requested and effective effort in execution identity, so effort-mismatched
runs refuse to fold — the same mechanism that already refuses mixed
toolchains.

### Three backends, three exams {#sec-parity}

A read-only audit of the harness, posted in full to the tracking issue,
found a deeper asymmetry: the three encoder paths did not administer the
same exam. The codex path ran in a workspace and could shell-read the full
context files. The Claude path ran prompt-only, with no tools. The OpenAI
API path — not on the standing roster — truncated each context file to a
6,000-character prefix silently, and capped output at 16,384 tokens
including reasoning, with partial artifacts eligible for scoring. CLI
versions went unrecorded, and version drift changes which flags a CLI even
accepts.

None of this shows on a leaderboard cell, and all of it shapes scores. The
v1–v3 cross-family readings above therefore compare models on different
evidence, and this paper flags them as weaker than the within-family
readings wherever they appear.

The parity encoder closes the gap by construction rather than by
calibration: every backend receives identical prompt bytes with all context
inlined; the codex workspace starts empty; context overflow fails loudly as
an infrastructure error instead of truncating silently; the harness rejects
partial or truncated artifacts instead of scoring them; undeclared file
access terminates the case; and CLI versions preflight and record per row.

### Case 04, flagged and retracted {#sec-case04}

All `{python} str(r.case04_fails_v1_v2)` model-runs across boards v1 and
v2 failed `income_tax_rate_bands`, and the v2 record flagged it as a
suspected suite defect: at zero for ten, a broken fixture explained the
data at least as well as a hard provision. Board v3 answered —
`{python} case04_passers` both passed it — and we retracted the flag on the
tracking issue the day the board posted. Ten consecutive failures had
measured difficulty, not validity. The operating rule the
episode set: unanimous failure justifies reading the artifacts, never
disqualifying the case from a summary table.

### Integrity notes {#sec-integrity}

The archived boards carry two integrity notes. opus-5's first v2 run
returned 1/16 with nine cases erroring in about a second each: its encoder
and its own reviewer drew on one subscription account, and the account hit
its session limit. We discarded that run as a measurement failure, split
the accounts, and re-ran clean — zero quota errors, case durations of 10 to
465 seconds, and the executed model verified from traces; only the clean
row ever published. luna's v2 advisory-review column covered 8 of 16 after
the shared reviewer account hit its own limit mid-run; the deterministic
gates read only compile, tests, and grounding, so its gate column stood.
Both events taught the same operating rule: an encoder never shares an
account with its own judge.

## Board v4, pre-registered

Board v4 runs when the parity encoder merges, and its design is fixed
before any result exists:

- **Same sixteen cases, same corpus release, new encoder** — a new board by
  construction, folded by the same contract.
- **One exam.** Identical prompt bytes on every backend, context inlined,
  empty workspaces, overflow loud, partials rejected, undeclared access
  terminal, CLI versions recorded per row (@sec-parity).
- **Effort as a recorded axis.** Codex arms swept at declared,
  receiver-verified levels; Claude arms at their adaptive default,
  disclosed as such (@sec-effort). Effort-mismatched runs refuse to fold.
- **Repeated runs per arm on the pinned encoder, reported as mean and
  spread.** Single draws retire (@sec-variance).

v4 is the first board eligible to support a cross-family capability
comparison. This paper refreezes with it: new snapshot, re-derived numbers,
same standing rule that no number appears here that the frozen artifacts
cannot reproduce.

## Limitations

Sixteen cases sample one jurisdiction on one corpus release; the suite
measures UK statutory encoding on this release, not encoding in general.
The gates check that an encoding compiles, passes its companion tests, and
grounds its numerics — they do not check full statutory fidelity, and the
oracle column that would cross-check computed results against PolicyEngine
UK stays empty until that runtime path is verified for eval cases. Each
(model, board) cell is a single run, so within-toolchain variance stays
unmeasured until v4's repeated runs. Costs are API-equivalents priced from
recorded tokens for the codex runners and CLI-reported figures for the
Claude runners. The runners are CLI products, not bare models: each brings
its own system prompt, tool behavior, and retry policy, and boards v1–v3
did not equalize them (@sec-parity).

## Reproducibility

Every number in this paper derives in code from the frozen run artifacts —
sixteen signed `results.json` files across the three boards, hashed
file-by-file in the snapshot manifest — through a results module that
re-implements the deterministic pieces of the `eval-board` fold. The module
verifies its derived headlines against the board records posted to the
tracking issue and refuses to render the manuscript on any mismatch; this
render passed that check (`{python} VERIFIED`).

[axiom-encode](https://github.com/TheAxiomFoundation/axiom-encode) holds
the suite manifest, the harness, and the fold; the boards post to tracking
issue
[#1189](https://github.com/TheAxiomFoundation/axiom-encode/issues/1189),
and
[PR #1304](https://github.com/TheAxiomFoundation/axiom-encode/pull/1304)
carries the parity encoder. The current board, the suite, and this paper
live at [encodebench.org](https://encodebench.org); the paper's source,
snapshot, and derivation module live in the
[site repository](https://github.com/TheAxiomFoundation/encodebench.org)
under `paper/`.
